strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in benchmarks by focusing on multi-day multi-POI intracity travel planning, which is more practically common than intercity planning
Comprehensive and realistic sandbox environment with authentic data from 10 major Chinese cities (720 flights, 5,770 trains, 12,192 POIs total)
Meaningful DSL contribution: composable design with 35 concept functions provides more scalability than TravelPlanner's 5 pre-defined concepts
Novel C-LPR evaluation metric thoughtfully ensures constraint satisfaction within realistic contexts, preventing shortcuts
Good integration of synthetic LLM-generated queries and human-derived queries, including unseen constraints in the latter
Thorough empirical study across multiple LLMs (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V2.5, Qwen2.5-7B) with oracle evaluation and ablations
Clear identification and illustration of three concrete challenges (DSL syntax, open language reasoning, unseen composition) with specific examples
Well-written paper with good motivation, clear figures, and comprehensive benchmark design
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: neuro-symbolic approach closely follows Hao et al. (2024) with nearly identical pipeline stages, primarily adapting existing methodology to multi-POI setting

Concerningly low absolute performance: best method achieves only 27.9% C-LPR on human queries, raising questions about benchmark calibration and solvability; no human performance baseline for reference
Heavy reliance on NL2DSL translation quality: large performance gap between oracle and standard modes (40.9% vs 27.9% for GPT-4o) indicates translation is the main bottleneck
Limited human query data: only 154 human queries (25% of total) after quality control, insufficient for robust statistical analysis or significance testing
Arbitrary methodological choices: 5-minute time limit for symbolic search, 90-minute activity durations, and 5 Reflexion rounds lack justification or sensitivity analysis
Insufficient baseline analysis: suspicious Act-only performance suggests potential implementation issues; Reflexion excluded due to cost; no comparison with optimization-based approaches
Language-specific and limited generalizability: primarily applicable to Chinese market; unclear how methods transfer to other languages or domains
Incomplete analysis of identified challenges: only one concrete example for open language reasoning; DSL's claimed compositionality doesn't fully solve unseen concept composition
Limited preference ranking evaluation: only 50 queries from already-solved set; insufficient for strong conclusions about preference optimization
Missing reproducibility details: no code availability timeline, limited implementation details for symbolic search, no inter-rater agreement for human query annotation

strengths: Well-motivated practical domain with comprehensive benchmark design including real travel data from 10 Chinese cities
Expressive domain-specific language that compositionally enables diverse constraint specifications beyond prior work
Integration of both LLM-synthesized (450) and human-derived queries (154) from questionnaires for realistic evaluation
Novel Conditional Logical Pass Rate (C-LPR) metric that ensures constraints are met within feasible plans
Clear identification of three concrete challenges (syntax compliance, open reasoning, concept composition) with examples
Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs with oracle translation experiments revealing bottlenecks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DSL is incremental extension of TravelPlanner; neuro-symbolic approach primarily adapts existing methods (Hao et al. 2024, Pan et al. 2023) with straightforward depth-first search

Undermines real-world claims with only 154 human queries (25% of benchmark) while 450 are LLM-synthesized; huge 60.6% vs 27.9% performance gap reveals synthetic queries fail to capture real complexity
Poor absolute performance (27.9% constraint satisfaction even with neuro-symbolic methods) indicates insufficient practical applicability; even oracle translation reaches only 35.0%

Significant scope limitations: Chinese-only reduces reproducibility for non-Chinese researchers; intra-city only (narrower than intercity TravelPlanner); only 10 cities raises geographic diversity concerns

Experimental design flaws: arbitrary 5-minute time limit unjustified; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-run error bars; oracle gap analysis only qualitative (Figure 4 examples, no systematic breakdown of failure mode frequencies)

Insufficient analysis depth: challenges identified but only anecdotal case-study analysis provided; no quantitative breakdown of failure causes; no ablation on neuro-symbolic components (verification vs. search contribution); preference optimization evaluated on biased subset (50 easy queries already passing)

Reproducibility concerns: recommends Chinese version but provides only English translations; implementation details scattered across sections with under-specified hyperparameters (why 90 minutes per activity? why 5 Reflexion rounds?); no clear commitment to release benchmark

Missing human evaluation: only 27.9% passing rate on human queries but no human judgment of actual plan quality, feasibility, or user satisfaction; cannot assess if passing plans are genuinely good travel plans

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real gaps in existing benchmarks: human-collected vs. LLM-synthesized queries show fundamentally different challenges

Comprehensive benchmark design with rich real-world data (10 cities, 3,413 attractions, 4,655 restaurants, 4,124 hotels) and careful quality control through manual verification and heuristic validation
Novel DSL approach with 35 compositional concept functions elegantly addresses scalability of fixed predefined concepts while enabling automated validation
Thoughtful evaluation metrics including new C-LPR that meaningfully distinguishes genuine constraint satisfaction from shortcuts/shortcuts
Rigorous experimental methodology: fair baseline setup (5-minute limits, oracle modes), multiple LLMs (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen), comprehensive ablation studies
Strong empirical insight: 10.7× improvement of neuro-symbolic over pure LLM methods (27.9% vs 2.6%) with systematic challenge analysis (syntax compliance, open language reasoning, unseen composition)
Extensive reproducibility support: detailed appendices with API specs, 35 concept functions, prompts, pseudo-code, and concept function implementations
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (Chinese-only scope, small human query set) without overclaiming generalization
weaknesses: Limited generalizability: single geographic/cultural domain (China only); only 154 human queries (26% of benchmark); 450/604 queries (74%) are LLM-generated despite quality control, risking persistent synthetic bias

Insufficient algorithmic novelty: neuro-symbolic pipeline adapts existing methods (Hao et al. 2024; Pan et al. 2023) with domain modifications; depth-first search with greedy scoring is standard; no comparison with sophisticated planners or alternative neuro-symbolic approaches

Critical DSL translation bottleneck: performance gap between standard and oracle modes reveals translation as fundamental limitation (e.g., 27.9%→35% on human queries) but paper offers no systematic solution; undermines 'compositional generalizability' claims
Low absolute performance on human queries (27.9% C-LPR) raises unaddressed question: is benchmark task unreasonably hard or are current methods fundamentally limited?

Claimed 'compositional generalizability' not rigorously validated: Figure 4 examples show failures but no systematic evaluation of compositional reasoning error rates; unclear how to handle requirements beyond 35 predefined functions

Preference evaluation severely limited: tested on only 50 seed samples due to low baseline FPR, undermining generalizability claims; PEQ sometimes hurts performance (P2) without investigation; no human evaluation of plan quality

Incomplete experimental analysis: limited LLM baselines (only ReAct variants); missing comparisons with recent methods; arbitrary design choices (90-minute activity duration, heuristic scoring functions) lack ablation studies; oracle translation is somewhat artificial

Benchmark construction relies on ad-hoc manual choices (meal time heuristics, rule-based activity selection) that are hard to extend; 4-stage quality control process is labor-intensive and doesn't scale
Unclear data/code release status: paper mentions support for global research but no explicit timeline or repository links provided

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing real limitations of TravelPlanner (synthetic queries, US-centricity, limited constraints)
Comprehensive benchmark design: rich sandbox with 12K+ POIs, three-phase data construction balancing authenticity and scale, and 1,154 human-grounded queries
Novel composable DSL framework with 35 concept functions supporting unseen constraint combinations; clear improvement from 10 to 100+ constraint types
Thorough empirical analysis: multiple baselines (ReAct, TTG, LLM-modulo, NeSy), new C-LPR metric addressing evaluation bias, detailed error analysis, and Chinese-context investigation
Excellent documentation: extensive appendices with reproducibility details, human subject protocols, DSL tutorials, and honest broader impact discussion
Clear identification of concrete research challenges: semantic POI reasoning (78.4% of queries), compositional generalization (12% accuracy on novel DSL structures)
weaknesses: Geographic and linguistic limitation to Chinese travel planning significantly reduces generalizability and applicability to top-tier venue seeking broad impact
Modest absolute performance: best method achieves only 37% constraint satisfaction; 63% failure rate raises questions about practical deployment readiness
Data composition: only 154+1000 of 1,154 queries are genuinely human; majority is LLM-generated, undermining claims about 'authentic open-ended human requirements'

Baseline implementation concerns: TTG requires aggressive downsampling (22 POIs, 1-hr discretization) yielding 18% valid solutions; LLM-modulo uses oracle verifier; arbitrary time limits (5/15 min) make fair comparison questionable
Limited technical novelty: NeSy Planning is straightforward depth-first search + LLM scoring; DSL is adaptation of existing ideas; main contribution is benchmark rather than methods
Unresolved bottleneck: large gap between oracle and standard modes (Table 3) shows NL2DSL translation is limiting factor, but insufficient analysis or solutions provided
Evaluation complexity: Table 3 difficult to parse; multiple metrics create interpretation burden; no inter-annotator agreement for DSL annotations

Incomplete analysis: DeepSeek vs GPT-4o performance gap (33.3% vs 23.3% FPR) only speculated upon; auxiliary POI reasoning task connection to full planning unclear; why smaller models fail so dramatically unexplored

Reproducibility challenges despite documentation: DSL annotations required only 3-5 experts (difficult to reproduce), questionnaire-based student recruitment, API simulation (not real), multi-stage construction with filtering
Limited human data validation: only 50 queries for preference studies; modest improvements in Figure 8 with insufficient explanation

strengths: Addresses real limitations of TravelPlanner with authentic Chinese travel data and 1,154 human-derived queries collected through rigorous quality control
Expressive DSL framework supporting compositional constraints with 88+ novel constraint types, enabling flexible and automated evaluation
Insightful analysis of open contextual reasoning challenge, showing 78.4% of human queries require semantic/cultural inference (vs. 5.4% in TravelPlanner)
Comprehensive empirical study across 6 LLMs and multiple NeSy approaches with detailed failure mode analysis and reproducibility details
Well-designed auxiliary task (POI reasoning) that isolates open language understanding from full planning
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—proposed NeSy Planning is straightforward depth-first search with LLM-based POI ranking, extending prior work [12, 20, 29, 28] without significant algorithmic contribution

Concerning absolute performance (23-37% FPR even on best subset) raises validity questions: are current agents fundamentally limited or is the benchmark overconstrainted? No human baseline or success criteria provided

Overstated claims and cherry-picked comparisons—'10× improvement' compares NeSy (52.6%) with one-shot ReAct (5.77%) rather than best pure-LLM baseline; '37% constraint satisfaction' presented as success despite implying 63% failure rate

Heavy reliance on synthetic data (1,000 LLM-generated queries vs. 154 human); limited analysis of synthetic bias despite claims of 'diversity'—auto-generated paraphrasing may introduce systematic patterns
Narrow scope limited to 10 Chinese cities with no human performance baseline, commercial system comparison, or cross-lingual/cross-domain generalization study
Fundamental issues underexplored: large oracle DSL translation gap (Table 3) suggests NL2DSL is the bottleneck, but implications for future work unclear
Dense presentation (45+ pages) with key contributions buried; Table 3 difficult to parse; inconsistent micro/macro metric differences large but underexplored
Low human subject compensation (1 CNY ~$0.14) with no inter-annotator agreement metrics; C-LPR metric feels like post-hoc adjustment to disappointing FPR numbers

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing clear limitations of TravelPlanner benchmark with compelling justification for single-city multi-day focus
Comprehensive benchmark design with thoughtfully engineered DSL for compositional constraint expression (35 concept functions enabling flexible combinations)
Substantial human data collection effort (1,154 queries from 250+ participants via questionnaires and survey platform) significantly enhancing realism beyond purely synthetic alternatives
Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple dimensions (feasibility, constraint satisfaction, preference ranking) with multiple baselines and detailed failure case analysis
Novel C-LPR metric addressing realistic evaluation concerns where agents might game systems by misreporting costs

Insightful identification of three key challenges (DSL syntax compliance, open contextual reasoning, unseen concept composition) well-supported with quantitative evidence (78.4% semantic POIs in Human-1000 vs 5.4% in TravelPlanner)
Excellent presentation quality with clear writing, well-motivated examples, effective visualizations, and comprehensive appendix with implementation details and prompts for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: neuro-symbolic approach represents straightforward adaptation of existing methods (TTG, LLM-modulo) without novel algorithmic contributions; NeSy Planning uses simple depth-first greedy search without exploring more sophisticated alternatives (beam search, A*, CSP techniques)

Scope limitations reduce generalizability: benchmark restricted to Chinese travel planning (though justified by market demand, raises questions about cross-lingual transfer); only 10 major Chinese cities; human data subset of 154 queries is small despite 1000 test queries

Evaluation concerns: results heavily depend on oracle translation modes (substantial gap between standard/oracle, e.g., 52.6% vs 46.1% FPR), suggesting NL2DSL is major bottleneck; 5-minute search limit appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis; lacking statistical rigor (no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests)

Incomplete analysis of why neuro-symbolic methods work: paper shows NeSy outperforms pure LLMs but doesn't deeply explore underlying causes; LLM-modulo comparison may be unfair (oracle verifier designed for different symbolic formalism); limited investigation of component contributions to performance

DSL limitations underexplored: Python-based syntax imposes learning curve with no usability study; 35 concept functions appear ad-hoc without principled design methodology; unclear how to handle requirements needing concepts outside predefined set; no discussion of expressiveness limits

Open contextual reasoning analysis lacks depth: auxiliary POI reasoning task is somewhat artificial (placeholder masking); binary Literal/Semantic distinction oversimplifies reality; performance degradation demonstrated but limited solutions proposed beyond problem identification

Missing comparisons and ablations: no comparison with other travel planning systems beyond TravelPlanner; limited systematic analysis decomposing difficulty factors; preference ranking evaluation shallow (50 queries, unsurprising finding that conflicting objectives are hard); TTG comparison may reflect adaptation issues rather than fundamental limitations
